diagnose-before-adapting.title: Choose the fix that matches the failure

sections.title: Do not train a model to memorize tonight’s menu
sections.content:
Your assistant writes too much, misses a newly added dish, and forgets the user’s current budget. Those are three different failures. A single “better model” decision can hide the actual cause.

Use prompting for task instructions and examples, retrieval for relevant external information, and explicit state for current user choices. Consider fine-tuning when a repeated behavior remains deficient after a sound baseline and you have suitable examples.

sections.alt: Instructions, retrieval, and model adaptation are different tools for improving an assistant.
sections.caption: Choose the intervention that addresses the observed failure.

sections.question: The assistant misses a menu item added today. What should you inspect first?

options.text: The data source and retrieval freshness.
The color of the chat interface.

sections.explanation: A changing fact requires an up-to-date source and a retrieval path that finds it.

sections.title: Separate changing facts from repeatable behavior
sections.content:
A daily price change belongs in a source of current data. A consistent output convention might be improved through instructions, examples, structured output, or eventually training. An incorrect total belongs in arithmetic code.

Fine-tuning changes learned behavior through examples; it does not create a live connection to a menu. Before investing, write down the failure frequency, the target behavior, the available data, and how you will measure improvement.

sections.title: Make an intervention memo
sections.content:
The Adaptation Lab presents specific failures. Choose an intervention and inspect the rationale, including why attractive alternatives miss the cause. This is decision practice, not a model benchmark.

Your memo should name a baseline, one change, an evaluation set, and a stop condition. For example: try two concise examples, then compare held-out requests. Escalate only if the measured shortfall remains important.

prepare-training-examples.title: Build examples that teach the intended behavior

sections.title: Examples teach both your intent and your mistakes
sections.content:
Suppose half your examples interpret “under $25” as item price and half as all-in cost. Training on both without a rule does not resolve the ambiguity; it teaches conflicting conventions. Define the desired behavior before collecting more data.

Each example needs an input, an expected output, and enough context to understand why the output is correct. Include corrections, unknowns, and edge cases rather than only perfect requests.

sections.question: Two almost identical versions of one conversation are in training and test. What is the concern?

options.text: The test may overstate generalization because of leakage.
The test is automatically more representative.
The model must fail because duplicates are impossible.

sections.explanation: Related examples can make held-out results look stronger than performance on genuinely new situations.

sections.title: Keep evaluation examples outside training
sections.content:
A training set teaches the behavior. A validation set helps choose settings. A final test set estimates performance on held-out examples. Near-duplicate conversations across these sets can create misleading confidence.

Split related examples together, such as variations of the same conversation. Remove unnecessary personal information and use authorized data. For this course, create fictional requests and keep your own final test cases out of prompt examples as well.

sections.question: Match each dataset to its role.
sections.explanation: Preserve a final set that was not repeatedly used to tune the system.

sections.title: Review the label before blaming the model
sections.content:
Take “No meat, but fish is okay.” Labeling it vegetarian loses the exception. A reviewer should preserve what was actually said, or ask for clarification when the format cannot represent it.

Write three examples in your reflection, then have a second pass challenge them. Are the expected fields supported? Do they encode the budget basis? Do they distinguish unknown from none? Label quality is a product decision before it is a training input.

understand-lora.title: Understand what LoRA and QLoRA change

sections.title: A small adjustment can be easier than rebuilding everything
sections.content:
Full fine-tuning updates model weights broadly. LoRA trains smaller adapter matrices while keeping the base weights frozen. Think of an adapter as a learned adjustment applied alongside the existing model, not a database of current restaurant facts.

This can reduce the trainable parameter count, but suitability still depends on the model, task, data, and resources. It is not a guarantee of higher quality. Hugging Face’s LoRA reference describes the method and configuration.

sections.question: What does LoRA primarily change during training?

options.text: Small adapter parameters while base weights stay frozen.

sections.explanation: LoRA learns parameter-efficient adjustments; it does not supply live operational data.

sections.title: QLoRA adds a memory-saving representation
sections.content:
Quantization represents weights with fewer bits. QLoRA combines a quantized base model with trainable low-rank adapters to reduce memory requirements during adaptation. It does not eliminate compute needs or evaluation.

Keep three questions separate: what is trainable, how base weights are represented, and how the result performs. A smaller memory footprint and a better task score are different claims. See the quantization guide.

sections.statement: Lower memory use from quantization guarantees better task quality.
sections.explanation: Resource efficiency and task quality must be measured separately.

sections.title: Decide whether an experiment is worth running
sections.content:
Our dinner prototype has no demonstrated training requirement yet. The exercise is to estimate the decision, not to download a large model blindly. Name the repeated behavior you want to improve and the examples needed to teach it.

In the Adaptation Lab, compare the recurring-format scenario with the stale-menu scenario. Only the former might lead toward fine-tuning after simpler baselines. Record quality, memory, latency, and maintenance as separate evaluation dimensions.

sections.question: Would you use QLoRA to fix a stale price? Why?
sections.sample_answer: No. I would repair the current data path. QLoRA adapts model behavior with a quantized base and adapters; it does not make a historical price current.
sections.explanation: Compare your reasoning with the sample. A different wording is fine if it preserves the decision and the evidence behind it.

compare-local-models.title: Compare a local model with your baseline

sections.title: Local execution changes the tradeoff
sections.content:
A local model can run on your own machine, but capacity, speed, and operational responsibilities depend on your hardware and the model. “Local” is a deployment choice, not a quality score. Check whether the full path stays local, including logs and optional cloud features.

Ollama provides tooling to run models and an API. Its official quickstart describes setup. Choose a model that fits your machine rather than treating a model name in a lesson as permanently current.

sections.question: What makes a fair local-model comparison?

options.text: Different requests for each model and guessed latency.
The same held-out cases with measured quality and timing.

sections.explanation: A controlled comparison holds the task constant and records real outcomes.

sections.title: Use the same cases and record actual measurements
sections.content:
The optional local-model runner in the lab bundle calls a local Ollama endpoint after you install and select a model. It sends one fictional dinner request and reports the actual elapsed time plus the response. It does not invent benchmark numbers or install software for you.

Run the same held-out requests with each candidate. Track field fidelity, invalid output, latency, and resource constraints. A fast response that changes the budget is not a successful optimization.

sections.statement: A local deployment automatically proves that all application data stays on the device.
sections.explanation: The surrounding application may still use remote services, logs, or optional cloud capabilities. Inspect the full data flow.

sections.title: Keep the live-model extension optional and concrete
sections.content:
Download the lab bundle, follow LIVE-MODEL.md, and use the provided command with your installed model name. If you are not ready to install a model, complete the decision memo using the clearly labeled scenario lab instead. Do not report simulated outcomes as measured model results.

Your final memo names the chosen deployment path, evidence, and remaining gaps. A beginner can make a sound product decision before becoming a model-training specialist.

sections.question: What would make you reject a faster model for this task?
sections.sample_answer: I would reject it if it loses budget or dietary constraints on the held-out cases, even if average latency is lower. I would also record malformed outputs and hardware limitations.
sections.explanation: Compare your reasoning with the sample. A different wording is fine if it preserves the decision and the evidence behind it.
